newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian court jails Venice belltower raiders.
newsitem.headline: Italian court jails Venice belltower raiders.

text.p: Eight men who stormed the belltower in Venice's St Mark's Square in a separatist stunt two months ago were jailed for up to six years by an Italian court on Wednesday.

President of the Court Graziana Campanato handed down sentences of six years to four of the men and of four years and nine months to the other four, after spending seven hours in a closed session with a panel of six lay judges.
The four jailed for six years -- Gilberto Buson, Flavio Contin, Fausto Faccia e Antonio Barison -- were immediately placed in custody.
The other four -- Cristian Contin, Andrea Viviani, Moreno Menini and Luca Peroni -- were put under house arrest.
The men were silent while their sentences were read out but Buson's wife, who was in the courtroom packed with friends and relatives of the defendants, burst into tears.
They were also ordered to pay 150 million lire ($88,000) in damages to the Venice town council and were all barred from holding public office for five years.
The eight, mostly in their 20s and 30s, broke into the belltower in the night after hijacking a ferry to take them and a ramshackle armoured truck to the square in the lagoon city.

Calling themselves soldiers of the "Most Serene Republic" of Venice which was for centuries an independent maritime power before its fall 200 years ago, the eight unfurled a flag of the republic and shouted separatist slogans.
Defending lawyers had pleaded for leniency after state prosecutor Rita Ugolini last week demanded sentences of up to nine years in jail.

One defending lawyer Luciano Gasperini told the court on Wednesday before the sentence was passed that the men had "acted in a spectacular way in order to make an impact on public opinion. A state should not be scared of ideas and of flags".

A local separatist politician, Fabrizio Comencini, who heads the Venetian League, said: "This is a sentence in the name of the Italian state, not in the name of the Italian people and certainly not in the name of the Venetian people."
The men had been charged with kidnapping the ferry captain, subversion, illegal weapons possession, threatening public officials and occupying church property.
Charges relating to the armoured car were dropped because the vehicle was not deemed capable of doing any damage.
The most serious of the charges, kidnapping for subversive ends, carries a maximum jail sentence of 30 years but was dropped. A lesser charge of straightforward kidnapping was upheld by the court.
